paras: The killing of George Bentley was the fatal shooting of a Black miner from Marietta, Georgia, by a white man named Sam Hunt at the copper mines in Haralson County, Georgia, in early July 1882. Hunt fled after the shooting, and two other miners were jailed over an earlier roadside assault. An Atlanta wire report presented Hunt as a constable who killed a miner resisting arrest, while Bentley's hometown paper described him only as a white man who returned with friends after losing a fight.

According to a Haralson-area account reprinted in the Savannah Morning News, seven Black men employed at the Tudor and Hart copper mines were returning from Rockmart on Tuesday, July 4, when they met a white man named George Weaver on the road. That account said three of them cursed Weaver "without any provocation on his part" and beat him with rocks, after which a warrant for their arrest was placed in the hands of Sam Hunt. The Marietta Journal gave a different prelude, reporting that Bentley had fought Hunt himself the day before the killing and that Hunt "was worsted."

Hunt came back the next morning, on what the Marietta Journal called "last Wednesday week," apparently July 5, and with "some friends" called on Bentley to surrender. In the Marietta account Bentley refused, "denying his right to make such a demand," and Hunt fired his shotgun into Bentley's side; Bentley died within a few minutes. The Savannah clipping instead said that when Hunt approached, one of the men drew a pistol and tried to shoot, and that Hunt fired first and killed him instantly.

Both Georgia accounts reported that Hunt fled or escaped after the shooting. Two of the miners, Bill Head and Jim Higgins, were arrested and jailed in connection with the attack on Weaver. Bentley's body was brought to Marietta on Friday morning and buried there. No report of an inquest, of Hunt's arrest or of any trial appears in the coverage.

The two Georgia accounts appeared first, the Savannah Morning News clipping on July 11 and the Marietta Journal's short item "Shot and Killed" on July 13; only the Marietta paper named the victim, calling him "a well-known Marietta colored man." An Atlanta dispatch dated July 13 then reached papers in Memphis and Wheeling on July 14, the Memphis Daily Appeal heading it "Killed While Resisting an Officer" and stating that "Sam Hunt, a constable, attempted to arrest seven colored miners." The wire version left out the fight, the victim's name and Hunt's flight, and some versions reduced the miners to two or dated the shooting to "yesterday."

As the item moved north into brief columns, the place name was garbled to "Harrison county," "Harrolson County" and "Harroldson County," and two papers moved the shooting to "Atlanta, Ga." and "Atlanta, Miss." A syndicated "Murderous Deeds" column printed in Minnesota and Dakota papers on July 19 and 20 gave the date as "the 13th" and named neither Hunt nor the victim.

The accounts disagree on whether Hunt acted as an officer: the wire called him a constable and the Savannah clipping said he carried a warrant, while the Marietta Journal described a personal quarrel and mentioned no office or warrant. The claim that the miner drew a pistol first comes only from the Savannah clipping, which also took Weaver's side of the roadside fight. Because the Savannah report of July 11 already described the killing, the July 12-13 dates in the wire copy reflect when the news reached Atlanta rather than when the shooting happened.

reader.title: Killing of George Bentley
bases: The wire and the Savannah clipping describe Sam Hunt as a constable or warrant holder shooting a miner during an arrest (A1, A3, A4), though the Marietta Journal calls him only a white man who came back with friends after losing a fight (A2).
Two independent Georgia reports (A1, A2) and the Atlanta wire (A3) agree that Sam Hunt shot dead a Black miner at the Haralson County copper mines and fled, though they differ on why and how.
